title: Babies receive everything
hookLine: in the East, infants are baptized, chrismated and given communion together

cards: The baby does not approve. She's been lowered into the warm water of the font three times, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, and she's letting the whole church know about it.
Then, still damp and wrapped in a towel, she's anointed with holy oil: forehead, eyes, nose, mouth, ears, chest, hands, feet.
And later, when the people come forward for communion, the priest lifts a small spoon to her mouth, a tiny portion of the consecrated wine. Baptized. Sealed with the Spirit.
Fed at the altar. All before she can say a single word.

teach.b: First, the three. Catholics call baptism, confirmation and the Eucharist the sacraments of initiation: the way someone is brought all the way into the Church.
The Catechism says plainly that in the Eastern rites, the initiation of infants begins with baptism, followed immediately by confirmation and the Eucharist.
In the East, confirmation is called chrismation, and the priest anoints with the words: the seal of the gift of the Holy Spirit.
Second, the West spreads them out. In the Latin Church, babies are baptized, and then come years of learning before first communion and confirmation later on.
The Catechism holds the two side by side and ranks neither: the Eastern way shows the unity of the three sacraments; the Latin way, by keeping confirmation with the bishop, shows the bond with him.
Same three gifts, different timing. Third, the reason the Catechism gives.

When it describes the Eastern churches giving communion to the newly baptized, even little children, it recalls the Lord's words, in the Douay-Rheims: "Suffer the little children to come unto me, and forbid them not."
Fourth, grace before understanding. A baby understands none of it.
Doesn't know the creed, can't say amen, can't even hold her head up. That's the point both East and West make by baptizing infants at all: grace is a gift, not a prize.
The East simply carries that logic all the way to the table.

how: In Eastern Catholic and Orthodox churches, an infant is baptized by triple immersion, chrismated with holy myron, and given communion from a spoon, usually in one celebration; Latin Catholics baptize infants and celebrate first communion and confirmation in later years.

o: babies are baptized and confirmed by a bishop
Eastern infants get baptism, chrismation and communion
every infant is promised to God at birth

games.q: all three at once — tap the pairs.

s: in the Eastern churches, babies receive communion
right after baptism and chrismation, from a spoon.
the Catechism says the Eastern way is the correct one and the Latin way is a mistake
it holds them side by side: one shows the unity of initiation, the other the bond with the bishop.
chrismation is a different sacrament from confirmation
it's the Eastern name for the same sacrament.

games.q: you're the priest. the baby has just been baptized and chrismated, and now the people come forward for communion. what do you do?
o: bless the baby, and wait until she's older.
give her a tiny portion from the spoon.
give communion to the parents only.
games.why: in the Eastern churches the newly baptized, even infants, receive communion. the Catechism links it to "suffer the little children to come unto me."

practice: Bring to mind a baby you know, or have held, or all the babies being carried to a font somewhere this week; then the tired parents, holding on, and the godparents who just promised something large.
If you pray, pray the Our Father for them slowly, the prayer they'll learn one day. If you don't, simply wish them well: a long life, and people who keep their promises.

wordCard.voice: Babies receive everything. In the Eastern churches, infants are baptized, chrismated and given communion in one celebration. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: an anointing, the oil of the seal of the Spirit.
